'''Fine-Art Nude Property — Image Sources, Licences, and the "Mr. Skin" Question'''

'''Status:''' research memo. Nothing in here is published, staged, or live. No wiki article, no
`site/` surface, no nav entry, no sitemap. This file is `.local/` (gitignored) by instruction.

'''Date:''' 2026-10-27
'''Prepared for:''' operator, MELEK/SoapBox

> '''This is not legal advice.''' It is a sourcing and rights-clearance research memo written by an
> engineer, from primary licence texts and case reports, for the purpose of deciding what to build.
> Several of the questions below (the right-of-publicity exposure in Part 2, and the §2257 analysis
> in Part 3) are the kind that a US media/IP attorney should sign off on before anything ships with
> money attached. Where I could not verify something, it says so rather than guessing.

---

== 0. The shape of the answer, before the detail ==

There are two completely different businesses in the brief, and they have opposite risk profiles.

# '''A fine-art nude gallery built on open-access museum collections''' is a ''solved'' rights problem.
   Several of the largest art museums on earth have put their public-domain holdings under CC0 — the
   most permissive instrument that exists — with explicit commercial permission, bulk downloads and
   public APIs. You can launch on this with effectively zero copyright risk, today, at zero
   licensing cost. The residual risks are not copyright at all (see §1.3 and §1.8).

# '''A Mr. Skin-style index of nude scenes in mainstream films''' is a ''live'' rights problem, and the
   risk is not where the operator's question assumes it is. The ''metadata layer'' — "film X, performer
   Y, timestamp 01:14:22" — is about as defensible as copyright law gets in the US (Part 2.2). The
   ''screenshots and clips'' are not (Part 2.4), and the ''performers'' are the real exposure (Part 2.5).
   Every convenient data source that would let you skip building the index yourself contractually
   forbids exactly this use (Part 2.6).

---

'''PART 1 — WHAT IS USABLE IMMEDIATELY'''

=== The three I would build on first ===

'''Metropolitan Museum, National Gallery of Art, Cleveland Museum of Art.''' All three are CC0, all
three state commercial use plainly, none requires attribution, and all three ship a machine-readable
dataset you can ingest in an afternoon. The Met's CC0 statement on the dataset is unambiguous — "To
the extent possible under law, The Metropolitan Museum of Art has waived all copyright" — and the
dataset page says the data may be used "in any media without permission or fee," including
commercially; attribution is requested, not required; the one hard prohibition is '''trademark'''
("You must not use The Metropolitan Museum of Art's trademarks"), which means: use the pictures,
do not use the Met's name or marks in a way that implies endorsement. Cleveland's API page is the
clearest of the three on commerce — "unrestricted commercial and noncommercial use" — and its
`share_license_status` field (`CC0` / `Copyrighted` / `Other`) gives you a machine filter, which
matters because the ''dataset'' is CC0 even where the ''image'' is not. '''Filter on
`share_license_status == "CC0"` and never on anything else.'''

The Met equivalent is the `isPublicDomain` boolean on the object endpoint. Same rule: the metadata
being CC0 does not make the image CC0. Honour the per-object flag.

* Met dataset + CC0 terms: https://github.com/metmuseum/openaccess
* Met Open Access hub: https://www.metmuseum.org/en/hubs/open-access
* NGA policy: https://www.nga.gov/notices/open-access-policy.html · dataset: https://github.com/NationalGalleryOfArt/opendata
* Cleveland API + terms: https://openaccess-api.clevelandart.org/
* Smithsonian terms: https://www.si.edu/openaccess · bulk: https://registry.opendata.aws/smithsonian-open-access/
* Rijksmuseum policy: https://data.rijksmuseum.nl/policy

'''Getty — verified, and it belongs in the first tier too.''' From Getty's own Open Content Program
page (https://www.getty.edu/projects/open-content-program/): *"Digital images of Getty-owned artworks
in the public domain marked with the CC0-public domain icon are available for download under CC0.
Such images are not protected by copyright and may be used without restriction or fees for
commercial and noncommercial purposes."* '''160,000+ images''' since 2013 — 86,000+ from the Museum,
including '''19th-century photography''', which is precisely the shelf that matters for Part 1.6, plus
78,000+ from the Getty Research Institute.

== 1.2 The quiet "no"s — where open access is not open ==

This is the part people get wrong. "Open access" and "the artwork is in the public domain" are not
the same claim as "you may use this image commercially."

* '''British Museum''' — images are offered under '''CC BY-NC-SA 4.0'''. The '''NC''' makes them
  '''unusable for a commercial property''', full stop. This is the single biggest trap in the field,
  because the BM has an enormous and heavily-digitised classical collection and it looks open.
* '''`NoC-NC` ("No Copyright – Non-Commercial Use Only")''', http://rightsstatements.org/vocab/NoC-NC/1.0/
  — used for public-domain works digitised under public-private partnerships where the partners
  contractually restricted commercial reuse of ''the digital file''. The underlying work is free; the
  scan is not. Appears across Europeana.
* '''`NoC-OKLR` ("Other Known Legal Restrictions")''', http://rightsstatements.org/vocab/NoC-OKLR/1.0/
  — no copyright, but cultural-heritage or traditional-cultural-expression law blocks free reuse.
  '''This is the statement that catches Italian holdings''' (see von Gloeden, §1.6).
* '''`CNE` ("Copyright Not Evaluated")''' and '''`UND` ("Copyright Undetermined")''' — these are the
  institution saying ''we don't know''. They are not a grant of anything. Treat as in-copyright.
* '''Flickr Commons "no known copyright restrictions"''' — https://www.flickr.com/commons/usage/ —
  explicitly '''not a warranty'''. Flickr's own page says participating institutions "often aren't the
  rights holders," give "no express or implied warranty," and tells users to "conduct an independent
  analysis of applicable law." Useful as a ''lead'', never as a ''clearance''.
* '''Harvard Art Museums''' — the API requires a key and the terms live behind a separate page; the
  data licence and the ''image'' licence are not the same thing (see §1.2a).
* '''Library of Congress''' — the largest pool of early American photography, and the most commonly
  misread. LoC states plainly that it "generally do[es] not own the rights to materials in our
  collections," that the researcher must determine and satisfy any restrictions, and that it
  '''does not grant or deny permission to publish''' and will not sign permission forms. Its catalogue
  note '''"No known restrictions on publication"''' means only that *the Library is unaware of any
  restriction* — LoC's own guidance states explicitly that '''it does not mean the image is in the
  public domain.''' The other notes are "Publication may be restricted," "May be restricted…", and
  "Rights status not evaluated." LoC asks users to do their own term analysis and to '''document the
  search as evidence of due diligence'''. Rate limit: no more than 10 requests/minute, honour
  robots.txt. https://www.loc.gov/legal/ · https://guides.loc.gov/p-and-p-rights-and-restrictions/risk-assessment
  '''Use LoC as a finding aid and then clear the item yourself on the §1.4 rules.''' That documented
  search is the thing that converts an LoC item from a lead into a usable asset.
* The full rightsstatements.org vocabulary (12 statements, 3 categories) is at
  https://rightsstatements.org/page/1.0/?language=en

'''Operational rule:''' maintain an allow-list of rights values, not a block-list. Only ingest items
whose rights field is exactly one of: `CC0`, `Public Domain Mark`, `NoC-US`, `CC BY`, `CC BY-SA`.
Everything else — including every `NC`, every `ND`, every `InC-*`, `CNE`, `UND`, `NoC-NC`,
`NoC-OKLR` — is rejected at ingest and logged. Record the source URL, the rights value and the
fetch date against every single image in your own database. If a claim is ever made, the provenance
record is the whole defence, and reconstructing it later is impossible.

== 1.2a Institutional detail — AIC, Yale, Harvard, Europeana ==

=== Art Institute of Chicago — metadata is clean, images are '''unverified''' ===

`www.artic.edu` sits behind a Cloudflare challenge that refuses automated fetching on every path,
including the IIIF `info.json`. `api.artic.edu` is open, and the API is authoritative on the data
side. The live `info.license_text` field (v1.16) reads: *"The `description` field in this response is
licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 Generic License (CC-By) and the Terms and
Conditions of artic.edu. All other data in this response is licensed under a Creative Commons Zero
(CC0) 1.0 designation…"* — '''metadata CC0, except `description`, which is CC BY 4.0.''' That is a
real trap: bulk-ingest the descriptions and republish them uncredited and you are in breach.

'''The images are expressly carved out.''' The docs say: *"For information about copyright, please see
the Image Licensing and Terms pages on our website. We defer to those resources in all legal
respects,"* and the `api-data` README repeats that the licence notices *"do not apply to images and
media which may have different licensing terms."* `is_public_domain` is AIC's belief about the
'''artwork''', not a licence on the file; AIC's own advice is to *"only using images from artworks
that are tagged as public domain"* and that *"it is up to you to determine whether or not you are
allowed to use these images."* Live count: '''62,119''' of 132,747 artworks flagged
`is_public_domain: true`. The IIIF manifest carries '''no `license` field''' and asks for the credit
line ''"Digital image courtesy of the Art Institute of Chicago."''

'''Secondary sources say AIC releases 50,000+ PD images under CC0. That could not be confirmed, and
the evidence actually reachable points the other way.''' API terms: no auth, '''60 requests/minute per
IP''', HTTPS, courtesy `AIC-User-Agent` header, and IIIF scraping guidance of one image at a time
with a ~1s delay. '''Treat AIC as unverified for commercial image use until someone opens
https://www.artic.edu/open-access/public-domain and https://www.artic.edu/image-licensing in a
browser.'''

=== Yale (YUAG and YCBA) — almost certainly fine, but they never say the word ===

Yale uses '''no named licence'''. Its formula (https://artgallery.yale.edu/terms-and-conditions,
https://artgallery.yale.edu/using-images) is that it *"provides free and open access to images of
works in its collection that are believed to be in the public domain,"* and that use is *"permitted
without further application, authorization, or fees due to the YUAG."* The 2011 Yale-wide
announcement was broader still: *"no license will be required… and no limitations will be imposed on
their use."*

'''Commercial use is not addressed either way.''' "No authorization, no fees, no limitations" reads as
permission, and I would be comfortable with it for most purposes — but Yale has not said the word,
and there is no CC tool to point at. Attribution is requested, not licence-conditioned
(''"attribute works and/or their images, without suggestion of endorsement"''). No warranty: YUAG
''"makes no warranties"'' on rights status. '''~154,000 works are IIIF-compliant'''; the downloadable set
is smaller. The '''Yale Center for British Art''' (https://britishart.yale.edu/terms-use) uses the
identical formula over ~70,000 PD images and is equally silent. '''If commercial use is load-bearing,
get it from Yale in writing. Do not build the business on an inference.'''

=== Harvard Art Museums — a clear NO, twice over ===

This is the one that surprises people, and it rules Harvard out of this project entirely.

'''The API''' (https://github.com/harvardartmuseums/api-docs) states, verbatim: '''"The API is for
non-commercial use only."''' Also: API key required; *"limiting the number of API calls to 2500 per
day"*; '''"You will not cache or store any content returned by the Harvard Art Museums API for more
than two weeks"''' without written permission; and '''"If you display images in your website or
application you must use the image URL returned by our API rather than create a copy on your local
web server"''' — hot-link only. Plus: link back, no HAM logo, no "harvard"/"ham" in your hostname,
free access to your app for them.

'''And there is a content clause pointed straight at this subject matter:''' *"You must not use the
API or Harvard Art Museums content in any context that is obscene, indecent, pornographic, illegal
or defamatory of any nature, or otherwise inappropriate."* That is subjective, unilateral, and HAM
reserves the right to cut access without notice.

'''The website images''' (https://harvardartmuseums.org/licensing) are *"available to download for
personal, noncommercial use."* Anything else goes through a request form and a bespoke licence:
non-exclusive, non-transferable, '''one use, one project''', publish within 2 years or it lapses,
'''materials destroyed after publication''', no cropping or alteration. '''There is no public-domain
carve-out on the page at all.'''

'''Net: Harvard is data-restricted, image-restricted, and carries a decency clause. Do not build on
it.''' The same caution applies to any institution with a morals clause in its API terms — read for
one before ingesting.

=== Europeana — the aggregator, and why you must filter per item ===

Europeana is '''not a rights holder and does not warrant anything''': the rights statement is set
per-item by the contributing institution. Querying Europeana's own Search API `RIGHTS` facet gives
the live picture across '''62,801,801 records''' — 65 distinct rights URIs collapsing to '''exactly 14
statement types''' (8 Creative Commons tools + 6 of rightsstatements.org's 12).

'''Commercially reusable:''' CC0 ('''8.03M'''), Public Domain Mark ('''11.0M'''), CC BY (7.6M at 4.0 plus
1.8M at 3.0 and ports), CC BY-SA (3.1M at 4.0 plus 1.55M at 3.0 and ports).

'''Not commercially reusable:''' CC BY-NC (1.12M+), CC BY-NC-SA (3.03M+), CC BY-NC-ND (3.72M+),
CC BY-ND (0.31M — derivatives barred; verbatim commercial use is technically permitted but it is a
poor instrument to rely on), '''InC — In Copyright (11.65M, the single largest bucket)''', InC-EDU
(1.72M), InC-OW-EU (1,146), '''NoC-NC (2.79M)''', '''NoC-OKLR (3.34M)''', CNE (0.36M).

Europeana does '''not''' use the other six rightsstatements.org statements (InC-NC, InC-RUU, NoC-CR,
NoC-US, UND, NKC). '''NoC-NC and NoC-OKLR are the dangerous pair''' — both say the ''work'' is out of
copyright while still barring or conditioning your commercial use. That is the scan-level assertion
pattern (§1.7) expressed as metadata. Access: Search API and Record API v2 at `api.europeana.eu`
(free key), plus IIIF and SPARQL endpoints.

== 1.2b Other European collections worth knowing ==

'''Clean and commercially usable:'''

* '''Paris Musées''' — '''CC0 Open Content''', credit lines read "CC0 Paris Musées / …". Live:
  '''413,339 works online, 420,243 PD images.''' API at `apicollections.parismusees.paris.fr`. This is
  the strongest French open-content source and the direct counterexample to the Louvre/RMN model.
  https://www.parismuseescollections.paris.fr/
* '''Nationalmuseum, Sweden''' — out-of-copyright works marked ''''PD'''': *"These digital images are
  public domain… you are free to use them however you like."* Crediting requested, following the
  Europeana Public Domain Usage Guidelines. Where the ''photographer's'' copyright still subsists the
  image is '''CC BY-SA''' — ''"for any purpose, even commercially"'', with attribution and share-alike.
  They route users to Wikimedia Commons first.
  https://www.nationalmuseum.se/en/explore-art-and-design/images/rights-and-reproductions
* '''SMK, Denmark''' — '''Public Domain Mark''', not CC0. Live via their API: '''203,745 records, of
  which 153,227 are `public_domain: true`''', carrying
  `"rights": "https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/"`. `https://api.smk.dk/api/v1/art/search/`
  PDM is functionally equivalent to CC0 for reuse, but it is a ''statement of fact'' rather than a
  waiver, and some downstream platforms treat the two differently. Record which one you relied on.
* '''Finnish National Gallery''' — '''CC0 on 36,000+ images'''; out-of-copyright images tagged
  ''tekijänoikeusvapaa'', in-copyright ones tagged ''tekijänoikeudet voimassa'' and sold through the
  paid image service. https://kansallisgalleria.fi/kuvapalvelu/

'''Not usable without paying:'''

* '''British Museum — CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. Confirmed.''' ~1.9M images released April 2020 under NC-SA;
  commercial licensing runs through '''bmimages.com''', which is live and paid. '''The NC bars this
  project and the SA bites even on non-commercial use.'''
* '''Musée du Louvre''' — verified from their own CGU (https://collections.louvre.fr/en/page/cgu).
  Art. 4.1.1.2(a): free reuse of medium-format photographs of out-of-copyright works only *"for any
  non-collective use within a strictly private context"* and an exhaustive list of museographic,
  scientific and educational purposes, with print publication '''capped at 1,500 copies''', mandatory
  credits and a permalink. Art. 4.1.1.2(b): *"any commercial use… must be the subject of a written
  request… to Rmn-GP via photo.rmn.fr"*, '''granted against payment'''. The '''text and metadata''' are
  separate and far more open — '''Etalab Open Licence''', worldwide, perpetual, royalty-free,
  ''"whether for commercial or other purposes."'' ADAGP-managed works additionally carry an '''express
  prohibition on text and data mining for AI training'''.
* '''Musée d'Orsay''' and '''BnF/Gallica''' — both refused automated fetching; '''terms unverified this
  session.''' The established position, to be re-checked by hand: Orsay licenses commercially via
  '''RMN-Grand Palais'''; '''Gallica''' permits non-commercial reuse free with the credit *"Source
  gallica.bnf.fr / Bibliothèque nationale de France"* but '''requires a paid licence for commercial
  reuse''', with "commercial" defined broadly. '''This is the biggest practical trap in the French
  material''' — the underlying photographs are unambiguously public domain and the fee is charged on
  the ''file''.

== 1.3 The CC0 trap: CC0 does not clear the person in the picture ==

This is the most important paragraph in Part 1 and it is the one most likely to be skipped.

'''CC0 waives the copyright. It does not clear personality rights, and it says so.''' CC0 1.0
Section 4(c): *"Affirmer disclaims responsibility for clearing rights of other persons that may
apply to the Work or any use thereof."* Section 1 lists *"publicity and privacy rights pertaining to
a person's image or likeness depicted in a Work"* among the rights in scope — but the Affirmer can
only waive rights '''it holds''', and a museum does not hold the publicity rights of the person who
sat for a 1925 photograph. Section 4(a): *"No trademark or patent rights held by Affirmer are
waived."* Section 4(b): the work is offered as-is, no warranties of any kind.
(https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/legalcode.en)

For a property of this kind, what that means concretely:

* A CC0 painting of a mythological figure: no residual problem. There is no identifiable living or
  recently-dead person.
* A CC0 '''photograph''' from an institutional collection where the sitter is identifiable and died
  recently enough for a post-mortem publicity right to run (Indiana and Oklahoma: 100 years;
  California: 70 years; Tennessee: potentially indefinite while use continues): '''the copyright is
  clear and the publicity right may not be.''' For pre-1931 photography this is mostly academic, but
  it is not zero, and it is the reason the gallery should favour 19th-century and early-20th-century
  material over anything mid-century.
* The same point kills the lazy assumption that a CC0 image is "cleared." It is cleared *of
  copyright*. Nothing else.

== 1.4 US public domain: where the line actually falls ==

Authority: Peter B. Hirtle, ''Copyright Term and the Public Domain in the United States'', Cornell
University Library — https://guides.library.cornell.edu/copyright/publicdomain — which is the chart
every US rights desk actually uses. As of '''2026''':

'''Published in the US'''
* '''Published 1930 or earlier → public domain.''' The 95-year term on a 1930 publication expired
  31 Dec 2025. '''1931 publications enter the public domain on 1 January 2027''' — roughly two months
  from the date of this memo, which is worth noting for launch timing.
* '''Published 1931–1977 without a copyright notice → public domain''' (failure of formality). This is
  a much bigger door than people expect for photography: a great deal of commercial and studio
  photographic output of that era circulated without a conforming notice.
* '''Published 1931–1963 with notice but not renewed → public domain.''' Renewal rates were low. The
  renewal records are searchable (Copyright Office registers; the NYPL/Stanford renewal datasets).
  This is the single most productive lane for photography, and it is also the most labour-intensive,
  because you must prove the ''absence'' of a renewal.
* '''Published 1931–1963 with notice and renewed → 95 years from publication.'''
* '''Published 1964–1977 with notice → 95 years from publication''' (renewal became automatic).
* '''Published 1978 – 1 Mar 1989 without notice and not registered within 5 years → public domain.'''

'''Unpublished works''' — this is where a lot of photographic archive material sits, and the rule is
different:
* '''Life of the author + 70.''' Unpublished works by authors who '''died before 1956''' are in the
  public domain as of 2026.
* '''Anonymous, pseudonymous, or work-for-hire, unpublished: 120 years from creation.''' Unpublished
  works '''created before 1906''' are public domain as of 2026.
* '''The §303 floor.''' 17 U.S.C. §303(a) gives unpublished works created before 1978 the life+70
  term but provides that it shall '''in no case expire before 31 December 2002''', and that if the
  work ''was'' published on or before that date, not before '''31 December 2047'''. That floor has now
  passed for the never-published case, which is why the "died before 1956" rule is the operative
  one today — but the 2047 floor still catches anything first published between 1978 and 2002.
* '''This resolves the hardest question in 19th-century photography in your favour.''' A great deal of
  académie and private figure-study material was never "published" in the copyright sense — it was
  studio prints supplied to painters and academies, or private-circulation albums. For any
  photographer who '''died before 1956''', both roads (published pre-1931, or never published at all)
  land on public domain, so the usually-intractable "was this ever published?" question becomes
  moot. For the French and Italian photographers in §1.6 — all of whom died before 1932 — that is
  the single most useful line in a clearance file.
* The practical trap: "unpublished" in US copyright has a term of art meaning. A photograph printed
  and distributed is published; a negative sitting in a studio archive, or a print shown only in an
  exhibition, generally is not. An uncatalogued archive photograph from 1925 by a known photographer
  who died in 1960 is '''still in copyright until 2031''' even though a published 1925 photograph is
  free. Archive provenance matters more than date.

'''First published outside the US'''
* '''Before 1931 → public domain in the US.'''
* '''1931–1977, published abroad without US formalities → public domain in the US only if it was
  already public domain in its source country on 1 January 1996''' (the URAA restoration date).
  Otherwise, 95 years from publication. '''URAA restoration is the thing that catches European
  photography''': a German or French photograph from 1935 that was still protected at home in 1996
  had its US copyright ''restored'' and is not free here, even though it fails the US formalities.
* '''The URAA line has moved, and most reference material is now stale.''' Per US Copyright Office
  Circular 38B (https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ38b.pdf), a restored work gets *"the remainder
  of the term of copyright that the work would have enjoyed if the work had never entered the public
  domain"* — for pre-1978 publication, '''95 years from first publication'''. A restored term on a
  '''1930''' foreign publication therefore expired '''31 December 2025'''. '''As of 2026, pre-1931 first
  publication abroad is US public domain even with URAA restoration; the URAA bite now begins at
  1931 and rolls forward a year each year.''' Cornell's footnote still warns about "foreign works
  published after 1928," and several Wikimedia Commons URAA warning templates are correspondingly
  two years out of date. '''Do not let a stale template talk you out of a clear 1929 or 1930 work.'''

== 1.5 Non-US regimes, and why the term differs per photographer ==

* '''EU / UK: life of the author + 70 years''', harmonised by Directive 2006/116/EC. The term attaches
  to the '''photographer's death date''', not the picture's date — which is why there is no single
  "European cut-off" and why each photographer has to be assessed individually. A photographer who
  made a picture in 1890 and died in 1950 is in copyright in the EU until '''1 January 2021'''; a
  photographer who made a picture in 1920 and died in 1925 was free in '''1996'''.
* '''Germany''' additionally distinguishes ''Lichtbildwerke'' (photographic works, life+70) from
  ''Lichtbilder'' (simple photographs, 50 years from publication) — a genuinely useful distinction for
  mass-produced studio and postcard material of the 1900s–1920s.
* '''The rule of the shorter term''' applies in most of the EU to non-EU works but '''not in the US''',
  which is why a work can be free in France and protected in the United States. If the property
  serves a global audience, the governing analysis is the '''most restrictive''' jurisdiction you
  intend to serve, not the US.
* '''Italy''' is a special case that matters directly here — see von Gloeden, §1.6.

== 1.6 Early art-nude photography: what is actually free ==

This is the shelf the operator actually wants, and it sorts cleanly into three groups. Works below
are figure studies / académies / nude studies in the art-historical sense; the question here is
purely one of copyright term and sourcing.

=== 1.6.1 The clean shelf — US public domain, solid ===

'''Eadweard Muybridge, ''Animal Locomotion'' (1887).''' Life 1830–1904. Photographed 1884–86 at the
University of Pennsylvania, published 1887 by J.B. Lippincott, Philadelphia — '''781 collotype plates
in 11 volumes''', human figure studies in Volumes I–IV. US publication, 95-year term expired 1982, no
URAA question, uncontested. The printed "Copyright, 1887, by Eadweard Muybridge" notice on the
plates has no current force. '''Best source: Wellcome Collection, which applies an explicit Public
Domain Mark''' — the cleanest rights statement of any Muybridge digitisation
(e.g. https://wellcomecollection.org/works/fc73mpfv). Also: Boston Public Library's 290-file set on
Commons (incomplete — missing plates 281, 321, 345–348, 431, 529, 551;
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Photographs_by_Muybridge_in_the_Boston_Public_Library),
Smithsonian American Art Museum (15 files), PAFA, USC/Calisphere, DPLA, and the Commons hub at
https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Animal_Locomotion. Penn's plate catalogue (subject,
model, movement type, camera angles, intervals) is at
https://archives.upenn.edu/digitized-resources/docs-pubs/muybridge/catalogue — '''but carries no
item-level rights statement, only a site-wide "© 2026" footer'''; boilerplate rather than a claim,
but ambiguous. Prefer Wellcome.

'''The French académies — Moulin, Marconi, Igout, Durieu. All US PD, solid.''' All four died before
1886; work dates 1850s–1880s; PD on both the published and unpublished tracks (§1.4); nothing was
still protected in France on 1 Jan 1996, so no URAA issue. '''The clearance risk in this group is not
the term — it is the institutional terms-of-use on the digital file, and the near-absence of CC0 at
French public institutions.'''
* '''Félix-Jacques Moulin''' (1802 – 1875; '''death date genuinely contested''' — some records say
  "after 1869", so do not state 1875 flatly). Paris studio from 1849; prosecuted 1851; 1856–58
  government-funded Algeria commission. Held: '''Getty Research Institute, 21 albumen photographs,
  accession 2022.R.2''' (https://oac.cdlib.org/findaid/ark:/13030/c8x92jr7/) — and Getty is CC0,
  which makes this the best-positioned of the group. Also National Galleries of Scotland; Commons
  https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Félix-Jacques_Moulin (35 members).
* '''Gaudenzio Marconi''' (1841–1885). Académies sold to artists and academies; Brussels from the
  1870s; best known for the 1877 study of Auguste Neyt, Rodin's model for ''L'Âge d'airain''. '''No
  main Commons category'''; ~98 file hits under "Photographs of nude males by Gaudenzio Marconi",
  sourced from '''Cleveland''' (e.g. 1996.357), ENSBA Paris, Europeana, Getty and auction houses.
* '''Louis Jean-Baptiste Igout''' (1837 – ''ca.'' 1881). The '''Album d'Études–Poses''', c.1880, albumen
  prints, issued by A. Calavas, Paris. '''Best rights position in the group: the Met, accession
  1993.270, returns `isPublicDomain: true`''' — https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/266917
  Also Rijksmuseum RP-F-2001-4-34 (download offered but '''no explicit licence on the record''' —
  verify), MFA Boston, MFAH. Commons: 26 files, '''no category-level PD tag'''.
* '''Eugène Durieu''' (1800–1874; dates confirmed precisely). Took up photography 1849; the relevant
  studies date '''1853–1856''', including the 1853 series made '''with Eugène Delacroix''', who painted
  from several of Durieu's models. In 1857 Durieu gave the set to the '''Société française de
  photographie''', describing them as ''"portraits et études d'après nature"'' — the key primary
  holding, though no SFP catalogue URL could be reached. Also Getty, the Met, Musée d'Orsay, SFMOMA,
  NGA. Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Jean_Louis_Marie_Eugène_Durieu (the
  shorter "Eugène Durieu" category is an empty redirect).

''Why so much of this survives, catalogued and datable:'' French '''dépôt légal''' was extended to
photography in '''1851''', exactly when the académie trade industrialised. Deposit was how you
established property in an image and sued copyists, so the studios had a direct commercial motive to
deposit. Deposit copies were accessioned as administrative records rather than as art — which is why
a semi-clandestine, frequently prosecuted genre survives in attributed, dated form. '''A deposited
académie carries a registration date, which is unusually good provenance evidence.''' (The 1851
extension itself is well attested; the finer claims about which department received them, and the
anti-copying motive, are the standard account in the photo-history literature but were not verified
to a primary source.)

'''Wilhelm von Gloeden (1856–1931) and Wilhelm von Plüschow (commonly 1852–1930, life dates
unverified).''' Gloeden worked in Taormina from the late 1870s; relevant work c.1890–1920s. '''US PD
is solid as of 2026, and that is recent''' — Commons still carries URAA warnings on his category
because the Italian term ran to end-2001 and so he was not PD at source on 1 Jan 1996. '''That
warning is now spent:''' the restored term is 95 years from publication, which has run for anything
published 1930 or earlier, and unpublished material cleared §303 on 1 Jan 2003. Italy and Germany:
PD since 1 Jan 2002. '''Residual edge case: a plate ''first'' published 1931 or later is still in a
95-year US term — document the publication date per image.''' Plüschow follows the same reasoning.
* ''Two sourcing notes.'' The Met's artist record misprints Gloeden's birth year as '''1886''' (should be
  1856). And the Met marks its Gloeden prints `isPublicDomain: false` with no image, for works dated
  '''1902 and 1903''' (acc. 2015.400.626, 2015.400.635) — on the Met's own arithmetic those are US PD.
  That is the Met declining to open-license its ''file'', not asserting copyright, but the practical
  effect is the same: '''no Open Access route.''' Better routes: the
  '''Magnus-Hirschfeld-Gesellschaft via museum-digital, which applies the Public Domain Mark'''
  (https://term.museum-digital.de/md-de/persinst/268045), ICP, and Commons
  (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Wilhelm_von_Gloeden, 37 subcategories). The Royal
  Academy routes commercial use through its Picture Library.
* ''Plüschow has no main Commons category and the spelling splits'' — searching only "Plüschow" misses
  roughly half the files, which are filed under "Plueschow". Search both.
* '''The widely-repeated claim that Alinari holds a large body of Gloeden plates could not be
  confirmed''' and should not be relied on. What ''is'' confirmed is that Alinari asserts blanket
  rights over its holdings under L. 633/41.

'''F. Holland Day (1864–1933) — solid on both tracks, and one of the safest names on the list.''' All
published work predates 1931, and he died in 1933 (before 1956), so unpublished material cleared
life+70 in 2003. EU PD since 1 Jan 2004. '''Library of Congress Prints & Photographs holds the
largest collection''' (~690 prints from his estate, much of it in the Louise Imogen Guiney
Collection), with the rights advisory '''"No known restrictions on publication"''' — e.g.
https://www.loc.gov/item/2004666555/ (fetch the `?fo=json` form; the HTML page blocks bots). Also
MoMA and Cleveland. Commons: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Fred_Holland_Day (251 files
in the "Photographs by" subcategory).

'''Clarence H. White (1871–1925) — solid on both tracks.''' Everything predates 1931; died 1925, so
unpublished cleared 1995. EU PD since 1996. '''Cleanest usable source: Cleveland Museum of Art, 81
works, all `share_license_status: CC0`''' (e.g. https://clevelandart.org/art/1980.129,
/1989.405, /1980.159). Princeton holds '''The Clarence H. White Collection''' (bequest 1983, accession
series `x1983-…`, artist → son → museum) — '''but Princeton's object API exposes no rights field at
all and no published image-rights policy could be found. Unknown; ask them.'''

'''Alfred Stieglitz (1864–1946) and ''Camera Work'' (1903–1917).''' ''Camera Work'' was published in New
York 1903–1917, so '''every issue predates 1931 and the entire run — every photogravure, every
contributor — is US public domain''': Brigman, White, Day, Käsebier, Steichen, Coburn, de Meyer,
Annan, Demachy, all of them ''as published in Camera Work''. Stieglitz's own work is likewise solid,
'''including the late work''': he died 1946, before 1956, so the unpublished output (''Equivalents'', the
extended O'Keeffe portrait, the 1930s–40s New York pictures) cleared life+70 in 2016. '''The
rightsholder-side institution agrees''' — the Georgia O'Keeffe Museum states that works by Stieglitz
'''have entered the public domain''' (https://www.okeeffemuseum.org/about-the-museum/rights-and-reproductions/).
* '''EU is not uniform.''' The journal is not the unit of term in Europe; each plate runs on its own
  photographer's life+70. Stieglitz → PD 2017, but '''Coburn (d. 1966) → 2037 and Steichen (d. 1973)
  → 2044.''' A plate that is PD in the US may not be PD in the EU. Flag if any surface is EU-facing.
* '''Two corrections to a common assumption.''' (1) '''The Met does ''not'' have a complete open-access
  ''Camera Work''.''' It catalogues the run, serves '''no images''', marks every issue checked
  `isPublicDomain: false`, and attaches an '''ARS © line''' to at least No. 29. It is not a sourcing
  route. (2) The '''Modernist Journals Project''' edition (https://modjourn.org/journal/camera-work/,
  scanned from Princeton copies) is the complete ''run'' but '''six images were torn out of the source
  volumes before scanning''' — Käsebier's ''Portrait (Miss N)'' and ''Red Man''; Dugmore's *Study in
  Natural History*; Steichen's ''Solitude'', ''Poster Lady'', and *The Photographer's Best Model: G.
  Bernard Shaw*. MJP also claims no copyright and then '''requires prior permission for republication
  or any commercial use''' — a terms-of-use overclaim on PD content (§1.7).
* '''Best sources:''' '''Cleveland''' (bound volume acc. 1995.199, CC0) and its '''Internet Archive'''
  mirror (147 "Camera Work" records, CC0 on the Cleveland-sourced items).
* '''One separate hook:''' the O'Keeffe Museum holds '''trademarks''' in the names "Alfred Stieglitz" and
  "Georgia O'Keeffe". Copyright has lapsed; '''the trademark can still bite on titling, branding or
  endorsement-style commercial use.''' Use the pictures, not the names as marks. (Same principle as
  the Met's trademark carve-out in §1.1.)

'''Anne Brigman (1869–1950) — solid, with one dated band to avoid.''' Her ''Camera Work'' plates (CW 25,
1909; CW 38, 1912) are PD outright; other pre-1931 published work is PD; and unpublished material
cleared life+70 in 2020. EU PD since 1 Jan 2021. '''The exception is 1931–1950 ''published'' work''' —
''Songs of a Pagan'' (1949) and 1930s–40s periodical appearances — which turns on notice and renewal
and needs a Catalog of Copyright Entries search before clearing (1949 + 95 = 2044 if renewed).
Cleveland holds 16 Brigman works.
* '''The claim that the Nevada Museum of Art holds a Brigman archive does not check out.''' NMA
  ''organised'' the 2018 retrospective, and '''its own page says the works came from the Wilson Centre
  for Photography, London''', plus other museums and private collections; Brigman is not among NMA's
  listed focus collections. NMA also asserts broadly over its own imagery — site images *"owned by
  the Nevada Museum of Art"*, personal non-commercial or fair use only, '''no public-domain
  carve-out''' (https://www.nevadaart.org/image-and-data-usage/). Not a source.

'''Albert Arthur Allen (1886–1962) — solid for the published portfolios only.''' Oakland studio 1916;
'''''The Female Figure'' Series I''' and the '''''Alo Studies'', 1919''', published by Allen Art Studios as
portfolios — genuine publication, all before 1931, and his productive period essentially ends with
the late-1920s bankruptcy, so most of the output sits inside the safe window. '''But anything
unpublished is in copyright until 1 January 2033''' (died 1962), and this matters more than it looks:
Allen was indicted for sending obscene material through the mail and spent years in litigation,
which means '''some work was deliberately not distributed''' and sits squarely in the unpublished
bucket. '''Be precise about which portfolio a given image comes from.''' '''EU: not PD until 2033.'''
'''Holdings could not be verified at all''' — no LC items, no Commons category, the Met's API returned
# The authority-control links on his Wikipedia page are artist identifiers, '''not evidence of
holdings''' — a common trap. Daile Kaplan's ''Premiere Nudes'' (Twin Palms, 2001) is the standard
published reference and the realistic way to date an image to a portfolio.

'''German Lichtbild / Freikörperkultur publications, 1900s–1920s.''' General rule: German works first
published '''1930 or earlier are now US public domain''', including under URAA; works first published
'''1931 or later''' were restored on 1 Jan 1996 for 95 years, so the 1930s shelf does not clear until
'''2027–2035'''. The EU side runs separately on each identified photographer's life+70, '''which is why
several of these are PD in the US and still in copyright in Germany.'''
* '''''Die Schönheit''''' (monthly, 1903–1931, Dresden; founded/edited by Karl Vanselow, then Richard A.
  Giesecke) — the first nudist publication to carry photographic figure studies. '''US: PD for
  1903–1930 issues; 1931 issues restored to 1 Jan 2027.''' EU: per-contributor, many pseudonymous
  (→ 70 years from publication, long expired). '''No complete open digitisation located.'''
* '''''Der Eigene''''' (1896–1932, Berlin, Adolf Brand) — contributors included '''Gloeden''' and Fidus.
  '''US: PD through 1930; the 1931–32 issues clear 2027–2028.''' EU: mostly PD (Gloeden d. 1931 → 2002;
  Fidus d. 1948 → 2019; Brand d. 1945 → 2016). Digitised at Humboldt
  (https://www.digi-hub.de/viewer/toc/BV042579260/1/LOG_0000/) — '''but the Humboldt scan pixelates
  the pages carrying photographs and artwork''', a library editorial decision, not a rights one. It
  is usable for the text and '''useless for the figure studies.'''
* '''Hans Surén, ''Der Mensch und die Sonne'' (1924)''' — 61 editions in two years, ~250,000 copies by
## '''US: the 1924 German edition and its 1920s reprints are PD.''' The '''1936 revision'''
  (''Mensch und Sonne – Arisch-olympischer Geist'') runs to 1 Jan 2032 '''and adds explicit National
  Socialist racial content quoting ''Mein Kampf'' at length''' — leave it alone entirely. '''EU/Germany:
  NOT PD — Surén died 1972, so his text is in copyright in Germany until 1 January 2043.''' This is
  the sharpest US/EU split in the set. The photographs in the book are by various hands on their own
  clocks.
* '''Gerhard Riebicke (1878–1957)''' — Berlin press photographer, sport and ''Freikörperkultur''; stills
  from the 1925 UFA film ''Wege zu Kraft und Schönheit''. '''US: PD for anything published pre-1931''';
  1930s publications restored (1932 → 2028, 1936 → 2032). '''Unpublished: NOT PD — he died 1957,
  ''after'' 1956, so life+70 runs to 1 January 2028.''' '''EU/Germany: in copyright until 2028''', and
  Commons tags his category `NoUploads until 2028`. '''German-market Riebicke images are commonly
  credited to a "Nachlass Gerhard Riebicke" — a credited Nachlass implies an active claimant on the
  1930s material. No contact was verified. Resolve before any use.'''
* '''Kurt Reichert — no term can be stated.''' Identity and life dates could not be established and the
  name collides with other German figures of the period. '''Do not clear anything under this name on
  the assumption that it patterns with Riebicke.'''

=== 1.6.2 The dated-source shelf — free only with a citable publication and year ===

For these, the law is clear and the difficulty is '''evidentiary'''. Dating the image to a specific
magazine or portfolio, issue and year ''is'' the clearance. '''Do not put any of these on a public
surface without that citation in the record.'''

* '''Alfred Cheney Johnston (1885–1971).''' Ziegfeld affiliation c.1917–1932; LC catalogues the studio
  work as ca. 1918–1939. Published pre-1931: PD. '''Unpublished: in copyright to 1 January 2042''' —
  and most of the figure studies were studio work, i.e. probably unpublished. Published 1931–1963 is
  renewal-dependent. '''The one genuinely favourable finding: Johnston donated 245 prints to the
  Library of Congress in 1960 (240 remain, LOT 8782), and LC's advisory on that lot reads "No known
  restrictions on publication for Alfred Cheney Johnston photographs in this LOT"''' —
  https://www.loc.gov/item/2005684587/ (items: /89712376/, /2008678879/; 61 items at
  https://www.loc.gov/photos/?q=Alfred+Cheney+Johnston). '''A lot-specific advisory attached to a
  deliberate gift by the photographer himself is the strongest clearance signal available here, and
  it is the route I would use.''' Commons reaches the same conclusion independently (493 files;
  `PD-old` not until 2042; `PD-US-expired` only pre-1931; warns most pictures cannot be reliably
  dated). After his death a cache of figure studies and glass plates was dispersed at auction to
  private collectors — note that '''owning a print or a plate is not owning the copyright''', though
  auction buyers do assert. No organised estate was found, which lowers practical risk without
  changing the term.
* '''Yva (Else Ernestine Neuländer-Simon, 1900–1942, German).''' Berlin studio from 1925; forced to
  close 1938; deported June 1942; declared dead 31 Dec 1944. '''EU/Germany: PD since 1 January 2013.'''
  '''US: URAA restoration genuinely bites.''' First published in Germany (''Die Dame'', ''Uhu'', *Berliner
  Illustrirte Zeitung*, ''Das Magazin'', c.1925–1938), never with US notice, never renewed — all four
  Circular 38B conditions met, so restored 1 Jan 1996 for 95 years from first publication:

{| class="wikitable"
! First published !! US expiry !! Status 2026
|-
| 1925 || 31 Dec 2020 || '''PD'''
|-
| 1928 || 31 Dec 2023 || '''PD'''
|-
| '''1930''' || '''31 Dec 2025''' || '''PD — only just'''
|-
| 1931 || 31 Dec 2026 || in copyright until 1 Jan 2027
|-
| 1935 || 31 Dec 2030 || in copyright
|-
| 1938 || 31 Dec 2033 || in copyright
|}

  '''Plus: unpublished Yva material cleared life+70 in 2013 and is US PD outright.''' Held at the
  Berlinische Galerie and Deutsche Fotothek. Her negatives are largely lost — 34 crates impounded at
  Hamburg in 1942, 21 destroyed in a bombing, 13 auctioned off — so the surviving corpus is mostly
  magazine tearsheets, which is conveniently also the evidence needed for dating. '''Get the
  tearsheet.''' No organised estate asserting rights was found.
* '''Biederer studio / Ostra-Studio (Paris, 1920s–30s).''' Jacques Biederer (b. 1887) founded the
  studio 1908; brother Charles (b. 1892) joined 1913; Éditions Ostra set up late 1930s. Czech-born,
  Jewish; '''both deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau and died in 1942.''' '''US: published 1930 or earlier →
  PD now; unpublished → PD (both died before 1956). 1931 onward is URAA-restored''' (1931 → 2027,
  1935 → 2031, 1939 → 2035). '''France/EU: nominally PD from 1 January 2013, with two real
  complications''' — (a) the French '''wartime extensions''' (''prorogations de guerre'', CPI L123-8/9),
  which the Cour de cassation has held are generally absorbed into the harmonised life+70 term
  '''except''' where a work already benefited under the prior regime; and (b) '''authorship and
  anonymity''' — much of the output was issued anonymously or under studio imprints, and an anonymous
  work runs 70 years from publication, '''but reverts to life+70 if the author is later identified,
  and the Biederers ''are'' identified in the literature.''' Both are questions for French counsel, and
  both must be resolved image by image on the specific imprint. '''There is essentially no archive,
  and that is the finding''' — the business did not survive the Occupation and the negatives were
  largely destroyed. What exists: Commons `Category:Biederer Studio` (59 files, '''no category-level
  PD rationale and no dates''', which is precisely the problem), private collections and the auction
  trade. The BnF's ''Enfer'' collection is the likeliest institutional home but a holding was not
  verified.
* Also in this band: '''Brigman 1931–1949''', '''Riebicke's 1930s work''', and '''Allen's undated studio
  material''', per §1.6.1.

=== 1.6.3 The no-go shelf — do not use without a licence ===

* '''Imogen Cunningham (1883–1976) — the Trust actively asserts, and it reaches further back than
  people assume.''' Cleveland records carry '''"© The Imogen Cunningham Trust"''' and
  `share_license_status: Copyrighted` on work from the '''1920s''' (e.g. ''Magnolia Blossom'', 1925,
  https://clevelandart.org/art/2019.23; ''Agave'', 1920, https://clevelandart.org/art/2024.167). The
  actual US position: died 1976, so '''unpublished runs to 1 January 2047'''; 1931–63 published is
  renewal-dependent and the Trust is exactly the organised successor that renewed. '''The only PD
  route is a work first ''published'' before 1931 — and publication means distribution of copies, not
  exhibition.''' Her earliest nude studies (c.1910) caused a scandal and she did not return to the
  subject for some fifty-five years. '''An exhibition is not a publication.''' You would be running a
  formalities defence image by image against a live, funded, actively-licensing rightsholder
  recognised by major museums. '''Do not put a Cunningham image on a public surface without a licence
  or a documented first-publication citation.'''
* '''Edward Weston (1886–1958) — the CCP ''owns'' the copyright. This is a genuine copyright claim, not
  a scan claim.''' The Center for Creative Photography, University of Arizona, lists '''Edward Weston
  by name under "Copyrights Owned by the Center for Creative Photography"'''
  (https://ccp.arizona.edu/copyright/copyright-permissions/), and the claim is doubled with ARS —
  Cleveland records carry *"© Center for Creative Photography, Arizona Board of Regents / Artists
  Rights Society (ARS), New York"* on work from '''1924''' onward. US position: died 1 Jan 1958, so
  '''unpublished runs to 1 January 2029''', and that is the controlling rule for most of the output.
  '''The chronology runs against you''': Mather/Modotti studies 1920–26, Bertha Wardell 1927,
  Noskowiak 1933, the Charis Wilson and Oceano Dunes series 1934–36. His pre-1931 ''publication''
  history is thin and mostly not the figure work, and '''his exhibitions are not publication.''' So
  the famous figure studies are almost all post-1930 and almost all unpublished pre-1931. '''US PD:
  no. EU: in copyright to 2029. The economics favour licensing.'''
* '''John Everard (British; real name Edward Ralph Forward) — the term is uncomputable, so treat as in
  copyright.''' Active 1923–1963 (one source to 1966); '''both birth and death years are missing from
  the standard reference records.''' UK/EU term is life+70, so '''with no death date there is no
  computable expiry''' — if he died as late as his last recorded activity, UK copyright runs to at
  least 31 December 2036. The UK unknown-authorship route is not available: "John Everard" is a known
  pseudonym of an identified person. '''US: all the books are post-1930 British first publications, so
  URAA restoration applies on a 95-year clock''' (1935 → 2031; 1963 → 2059). '''US PD: no.''' A failed
  US renewal on a US edition would be the only way out, and that is a research commission.
  '''Do not let anyone guess a death date to make this work.'''

=== 1.6.4 EU-facing caution — public domain in the US, not in the EU ===

If any surface serves Europe, these are in copyright there even where the US is clear: '''Surén's
text''' (to 2043), '''Albert Arthur Allen''' (to 2033), '''Weston''' (to 2029), '''Riebicke''' (to 2028),
and the '''Steichen (2044)''' and '''Coburn (2037)''' plates within ''Camera Work''.

=== 1.6.5 The Italian cultural-heritage complication — and how to frame it correctly ===

This gets described as "Italy claims copyright in public-domain works." '''That framing is wrong and
will mislead a reviewer.''' It is '''not copyright and not a term question''': it is an '''administrative
concession-and-fee regime''' under D.Lgs. 42/2004 (the ''Codice dei beni culturali''), arts. 106–108,
attaching to '''Italian State-held cultural property''' — a separate public-law permission layer with
contested extraterritorial reach.

It has been litigated and enforced: ''Ministero della Cultura v. Cave Michelangelo'' (Firenze, 11 Apr
2022, €500/day penalty); ''Gallerie dell'Accademia di Venezia v. Ravensburger'' (24 Oct 2022,
''Vitruvian Man'' puzzles, €1,500/day); ''Uffizi/Accademia v. GQ'' (Trib. Firenze, Apr–May 2023, '''€20,000
concession fee plus €30,000 for distortion''' over a ''David'' cover, grounding a "right to the image of
cultural property" in arts. 107–108 plus Art. 9 of the Constitution). '''Ministerial Decree 161 of 11
April 2023''' sets minimum fees, is mandatory for State museums, and '''removes their discretion to
release images openly under CC'''. Italy then inserted '''art. 32-quater''' into Law 633/1941 (D.Lgs.
177, Nov 2023) implementing DSM art. 14 '''while expressly preserving the Codice's reproduction
rules''' — i.e. Italy legislated the carve-out. '''Whether that survives art. 14 is unresolved''' and
has not been referred to the CJEU.

'''Practical read: this reaches you only if you source the image ''from'' an Italian State
institution's holding, or reproduce an Italian State-held object.''' Gloeden and Plüschow prints held
at the Met, Getty, ICP, Wellcome or privately are outside it. '''Sourcing matters more than subject
matter.''' This is also where Europeana's `NoC-OKLR` statement (§1.2a) mostly lives.

=== 1.6.6 Best actual sourcing routes for this shelf ===

# '''Cleveland Museum of Art's CC0 API''' — ''Camera Work'' plates and Clarence White. (Ignore its
   erroneous `Copyrighted` flags on pre-1931 items; see §1.7.)
# '''Library of Congress''' — F. Holland Day (Guiney Collection) and Johnston (LOT 8782). No rights
   claimed, no fees — but do your own term analysis and keep the record (§1.2).
# '''Getty Open Content''' — CC0, commercial explicit, strong in 19th-century photography; holds
   Moulin and Marconi material.
# '''The Met's `isPublicDomain: true` objects''', per accession number (e.g. Igout 1993.270).
# '''Wellcome Collection''' (Public Domain Mark) — Muybridge.
# '''Paris Musées, SMK, Nationalmuseum Sweden, Finnish National Gallery''' — European open content.
# '''Modernist Journals Project''' — a complete ''reading'' copy of ''Camera Work'', but ask before
   redistributing per their terms, and note the six missing images.

== 1.7 Bridgeman: the museum's photograph of a public-domain painting ==

'''Bridgeman Art Library, Ltd. v. Corel Corp.''' — note there are '''two''' opinions, and citing only
the 1999 one is standard but incomplete:
* '''25 F. Supp. 2d 421 (S.D.N.Y., 13 November 1998)''' (also 49 U.S.P.Q.2d 1091) — summary judgment
  for Corel, decided partly on UK law;
* '''36 F. Supp. 2d 191 (S.D.N.Y., 2 March 1999)''' (also 1999 WL 85513) — '''on reargument''', the same
  result reached under US law. Judge '''Lewis A. Kaplan'''.

Held: an exact photographic reproduction of a public-domain two-dimensional artwork lacks the
originality ''Feist'' requires, and so attracts no new copyright. Skill, labour and expense in
achieving an accurate copy are sweat of the brow; what is needed is an independent creative spark,
and a slavish copy by definition has none. The court adopted Nimmer's formulation that copyright is
denied where a photograph "amounts to nothing more than slavish copying," noting that "the point of
the exercise was to reproduce the underlying works with absolute fidelity." *(The full opinion text
could not be retrieved this session — Justia and OpenJurist refused automated fetching and
CourtListener's opinion endpoint requires auth. The holding above is accurate and uncontroversial,
but pull any verbatim quotation from the reporter before putting it in a document that matters.)*

Four things to hold about it:

# '''It is a district court decision.''' It binds nobody outside S.D.N.Y. It is widely followed and
   was cited approvingly by the Tenth Circuit in *Meshwerks, Inc. v. Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A.,
   Inc.*, 528 F.3d 1258 (10th Cir. 2008), but it has never been affirmed by the Supreme Court and
   there is contrary district authority (''Schiffer Publishing v. Chronicle Books'', 350 F. Supp. 2d
   613 (E.D. Pa. 2004), usually distinguished on the ground that those photographs were visibly
   ''inaccurate'' and therefore original).
# '''It only reaches 2D works.''' A photograph of a ''sculpture'' involves lighting, angle and framing
   choices and is an original work in its own right. Half of the classical nude material in these
   collections is sculpture. '''Do not assume Bridgeman clears a photograph of a statue.''' Rely on
   the institution's own CC0 grant for those, not on Bridgeman.
# '''It does not defeat contract.''' This is the point that actually matters, and it is the one most
   often missed. An institution's terms of use, a click-through, or a licence you accepted in order
   to obtain the file '''binds you as contract even where there is no copyright at all.''' That is the
   real mechanism behind nearly every scan-level assertion catalogued in this memo — the Met
   withholding Open Access files on PD objects, the Modernist Journals Project's permission
   requirement, Gallica's commercial fee, the Louvre's RMN route, the Nevada Museum of Art's claim.
   '''Bridgeman kills the copyright claim and leaves the contract claim standing.'''
# '''The UK has caught up, and the EU has legislated.''' In the UK, ''THJ Systems v. Sheridan'' [2023]
   EWCA Civ 1354 (Arnold LJ) confirms no new copyright arises from a photographic reproduction of a
   2D public-domain artwork; the UK IPO's guidance says the same. In the EU, '''Article 14 of the DSM
   Directive (Directive (EU) 2019/790)''' provides, verbatim:

   > Member States shall provide that, when the term of protection of a work of visual art has
   > expired, any material resulting from an act of reproduction of that work is not subject to
   > copyright or related rights, unless the material resulting from that act of reproduction is
   > original in the sense that it is the author's own intellectual creation.

   https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/790/oj (CELEX 32019L0790; OJ L 130, 17.5.2019, pp. 92–125)

   Article 14 bars new copyright '''and related rights''', which is what closes the German
   ''Lichtbild'' route (§72 UrhG — the basis of the Reiss-Engelhorn-Museen litigation) and is the part
   that actually mattered. '''But read the last sentence of Recital 53:''' *"All of that should not
   prevent cultural heritage institutions from selling reproductions, such as postcards."* That is
   the loophole everyone uses. Article 14 improved the ''legal'' position without much changing the
   ''practical'' one — the practice simply migrated from copyright to contract, access control, and in
   Italy to public-law concession (§1.6.5).

'''Practical consequence, stated carefully:''' for a 2D painting, drawing or photographic print in the
public domain, the museum's scan carries no new copyright in either the US or the EU, *regardless of
what the museum's website says*. '''But the remaining exposure on both sides of the Atlantic is
contractual and administrative, not copyright''' — and a terms-of-use breach is a cheaper and easier
claim for an institution to bring than an infringement suit. So '''do not build on Bridgeman.'''
Relying on it means relying on an unaffirmed district court case against a well-resourced
institution with a contrary written policy you probably clicked through. There are several hundred
thousand CC0 images available where the institution has already conceded the point. Use those, and
keep Bridgeman as a defence rather than a sourcing strategy.

== 1.8 Contemporary work under Creative Commons ==

=== What CC BY 4.0 actually obliges a commercial site to do ===

CC BY 4.0 permits commercial use — the licence grant is "worldwide, royalty-free, non-exclusive,
irrevocable" and contains no non-commercial restriction. In exchange, '''Section 3(a)(1)''' requires,
every time you share the material:

# identify the '''creator''' (and anyone else the licensor designates), by pseudonym if designated;
# retain any '''copyright notice''' supplied;
# retain a reference to the '''licence''';
# retain a reference to the '''warranty disclaimer''';
# include a '''URI or hyperlink to the material''', where reasonably practicable;
# '''state whether you modified it''', and retain any prior modification notices;
# state that the material is licensed under CC BY 4.0, with its text or a link.

Section 3(a)(2) lets you satisfy all of that "in any reasonable manner based on the medium, means,
and context" — in practice a per-image credit line and a credits page, not seven lines under every
picture. (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/legalcode.en)

'''The teeth: Section 6(a) terminates your rights automatically on any failure to comply.''' Not on
notice — automatically. Section 6(b) reinstates them if you cure within 30 days of ''discovering'' the
violation, but reinstatement does not extinguish the licensor's claim for the period of breach. A
commercial gallery that drops the credit line on 400 CC BY images has, technically, 400 unlicensed
reproductions. '''This is a build requirement, not a content requirement:''' the credit must be
generated from the database record, mechanically, and must be impossible to publish without.

'''CC BY-SA 4.0''' adds ShareAlike: adaptations must be released under the same licence. For a gallery
that ''displays'' images unmodified, SA is largely inert — mere collection in a gallery is not an
adaptation. It bites the moment you crop, recolour, composite, or build derived works, at which
point the derivative must itself go out under BY-SA. '''That is usually incompatible with a paid
property''', because it means your derived asset must be freely redistributable by your subscribers.
Rule: BY-SA images get displayed as-is or not at all.

'''CC licences are irrevocable''' once granted — a licensor can stop distributing under the licence,
but copies already out stay licensed. That cuts in your favour, provided you can prove the licence
that applied on the day you took it. Snapshot the licence state at ingest.

=== CC BY-NC: unusable. Say it plainly. ===

'''Any `NC` variant — CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA, CC BY-NC-ND — is unusable for a commercial property.'''
Not "risky," not "grey": the licence does not grant the right you need. A subscription site, an
ad-supported site, or a free site that exists to funnel traffic to a paid product is commercial use.
There is no safe-harbour reading. If you want an NC-licensed image, you negotiate a separate licence
with the rightsholder, which is exactly what the NC term exists to make you do.

Same for '''`ND` (NoDerivatives)''': no cropping, no colour correction, no thumbnails that alter the
image, no compositing. For a gallery that does any layout work at all, ND is more trouble than it is
worth. Exclude it at ingest alongside NC.

=== Where contemporary CC BY / CC BY-SA work actually lives ===

* '''Wikimedia Commons''' — policy requires every accepted file to be under a licence permitting
  '''republication, derivative works and commercial use''', perpetual and irrevocable. NC and ND are
  '''forbidden''' unless the file also carries an acceptable free licence. That makes Commons the
  single most reliable pool, but note: the obligation to attribute is per-file, and the file
  description page's claim is only as good as the uploader. Verify the upstream source on anything
  load-bearing. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Commons:Licensing
''' Commons also accepts '''faithful reproductions of 2D public-domain artworks as public domain
    regardless of source country''' (the PD-Art position), which is Bridgeman applied as policy.
* '''Flickr''' CC-licensed uploads — filter strictly to BY and BY-SA; the API exposes the licence id.
  Treat the uploader's licence claim as unverified: Flickr has a large volume of
  licence-laundered material. For a nude-art property this matters more than usual, because
  misattributed images of identifiable people are the specific failure mode that generates
  complaints.
* '''Europeana''' — per-item, must be filtered (§1.2).

---

'''PART 2 — THE "MR. SKIN" QUESTION'''

== 2.1 What that business actually is ==

Mr. Skin launched '''10 August 1999''', founded by '''Jim McBride''', a former Chicago radio
personality; the corporate parent is '''SK Intertainment, Inc.''' (Chicago, est. 1999), which also
operates a male-nudity sibling site launched in 2013 and acquired another adult-adjacent property in
February 2014. Traffic was reported at 7M monthly visitors (2007), 10M+ (2014), 9M+ (2017).
Registration is optional for previews — i.e. a '''freemium/subscription model with a free metadata
tier'''. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Skin)

The structure is the thing to understand, because it is two products stacked:

* '''Layer 1 — the index.''' Title, year, performer, scene, timestamp, a short factual descriptor, and
  a rating. This is a factual compilation. It is the part that is genuinely hard to replicate and
  it is the part that is cheapest to defend.
* '''Layer 2 — the media.''' Hosted screenshots and clips taken from the films. This is the part that
  converts subscriptions, and it is the part with no clean legal theory under it.

'''How it has justified the media:''' by '''asserting fair use''' — McBride's public position is that the
site is "a compilation of reviews, references and other critical commentary on actresses and the
films in which they have appeared" — and by pointing to studio cooperation, claiming that "about
75-percent of movie companies and movie distributors send us screeners of their films." '''Both are
the company's own statements.''' I found '''no public evidence of any formal licence agreement with
any studio or distributor''', and '''no court has ever ruled on the fair-use claim.''' Sending a
screener for review is not a licence and does not estop anyone.

'''Litigation — one confirmed case, disposition unknown.''' *Creative Photographers, Inc. and
Lickerish Ltd. v. SK Intertainment*, filed in federal court in California in '''mid-January 2019''': a
'''copyright''' action by two photo agencies alleging unauthorised use of '''photographs''' to drive
subscriptions and ad sales. The docket and outcome could not be retrieved. Note what the claim was
''not'' about: not the clips, not the scene index — '''the still photographs it reproduced.''' That is
the shape of the risk in miniature.

I found '''no reliable sourcing for any right-of-publicity suit''' against the company. That is an
absence of evidence from a budget-limited search, not a finding that none exists, and given §2.5 it
would be unwise to read it as a clean bill of health. A PACER name search is the proper check.

'''Read the 26-year survival correctly.''' It is not evidence that the model is lawful. It is evidence
that the model has been ''tolerated'' — by studios who benefit from the publicity, and by performers
for whom suing is worse than being listed. Tolerance is not a licence, and the thing that changes
tolerance is a change in the law. Part 2.7 is that change.

== 2.2 Facts are not copyrightable — and a timestamp is a fact ==

'''Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991)''' is the controlling
authority and it is about as favourable as a case can be.

* ''"The sine qua non of copyright is originality."''
* ''"[N]o author may copyright his ideas or the facts he narrates"'' — which the Court calls '''"the
  most fundamental axiom of copyright law."'''
* The Court expressly held that '''"originality, not 'sweat of the brow,' is the touchstone of
  copyright protection in directories and other fact-based works."''' Rural had compiled its white
  pages at real expense; that expense bought it nothing.
* *"A factual compilation is eligible for copyright if it features an original selection or
  arrangement of facts"* — but ''"the copyright in a factual compilation is thin."''
* And the operative sentence for this business: despite a valid compilation copyright, '''"a
  subsequent compiler remains free to use the facts contained in another's publication"''' to prepare
  a competing work.

https://www.law.cornell.edu/supremecourt/text/499/340

'''Applied:''' the proposition "film ''X'' (1994) contains a scene involving performer ''Y'' at 01:14:22"
is a '''fact about the world'''. It is not authored, it is observed. Recording it, and recording
100,000 more like it, creates a factual compilation in which the facts themselves are free for
anyone — including you, and including anyone who later copies you. Independently observing those
facts and publishing them is '''not copyright infringement of the film''', and it is '''not
infringement of an existing index that records the same facts.'''

Note the second half of that: Feist cuts both ways. Your index will also be, as to its facts,
uncopyrightable. You cannot build a moat out of it.

== 2.3 The limits: selection and arrangement, and the EU database right ==

=== Limit 1 — original selection and arrangement ''is'' protected ===

Feist protects the ''compilation'' where the selection, coordination or arrangement is original, even
though every underlying fact is free. In practice that means: '''do not copy someone else's index.'''
Copy their ''facts'' — permitted — but not their taxonomy, their rating scheme, their categories,
their editorial descriptions, their ordering, or their choice of what to include and omit. The
descriptive prose attached to each entry is plainly original expression and is fully protected.
Wholesale scraping of an existing index and reskinning it is the way this goes wrong, and it goes
wrong on ''selection and arrangement'' plus ''the text'', not on the timestamps.

The safe construction: '''independently observed facts, your own taxonomy, your own words.'''

=== Limit 2 — the EU sui generis database right, which has no US analogue ===

'''Directive 96/9/EC on the legal protection of databases''' creates a second, separate right that does
not exist in American law. Two tiers:

* '''Article 3(1)''' — copyright, for databases which "by reason of the selection or arrangement of
  their contents, constitute the author's own intellectual creation." This is roughly Feist.
* '''Article 7''' — the '''''sui generis''''' right. It gives the maker of a database the right to prevent
  extraction and/or re-utilisation of all or a substantial part of the contents, where there has
  been '''"a substantial investment in either the obtaining, verification or presentation of the
  contents."''' It applies '''whether or not''' the database or its contents are protected by
  copyright, and it also bars '''repeated and systematic extraction of insubstantial parts''' where
  that conflicts with normal exploitation or unreasonably prejudices the maker's legitimate
  interests.
* '''Article 10''' — term: '''15 years''' from 1 January of the year following completion (or following
  first public availability, if later). A substantial new investment restarts the clock — in a
  continuously updated database, the term is effectively perpetual.
* '''Article 11''' — beneficiaries: nationals or habitual residents of a Member State, and companies
  formed under Member State law with registered office, central administration or principal place of
  business in the Community. Extension to third-country databases requires a Council agreement.

https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1996/9/oj · https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/1996/9/article/7

'''This is exactly the "sweat of the brow" doctrine that the US rejected in Feist, re-enacted as
statute in Europe.''' A US-only analysis gets this wrong in both directions:

# '''Downside.''' If you systematically extract substantial parts of an EU-maker's database, you can
   be liable in the EU even though the identical act is lawful in the US. Scraping a European film
   database is a different legal act from scraping an American one.
# '''Upside, and this is the part worth noticing.''' The CJEU's '''British Horseracing Board v.
   William Hill (C-203/02, 2004)''' draws the critical line: investment in '''creating''' the data does
   not count — only investment in '''obtaining, verifying or presenting''' pre-existing data. A
   database of facts you generated yourself is, on BHB, outside the sui generis right. An index built
   by '''watching films and recording observations''' is arguably ''creating'' data, not ''obtaining'' it,
   which means '''your own database might not attract the sui generis right at all''' even if you are
   EU-established. Conversely, ''CV-Online Latvia (C-762/19, 2021)'' requires a claimant to show that
   the extraction actually damaged its investment. Net: the EU right is a real constraint on what you
   may take, and a weak shield for what you build.
* '''Article 11 also means''' a US-incorporated maker gets no sui generis right in the EU at all. If
  this property is a US entity, it is exposed to the right and cannot invoke it.
* '''UK post-Brexit:''' the Copyright and Rights in Databases Regulations 1997 survive. Database rights
  arising on or after 1 January 2021 are protected only within the jurisdiction of their creation —
  UK rights in the UK, EEA rights in the EEA — with reciprocal recognition preserved only for rights
  that existed before that date.
* '''The United States has no database right at all.''' Repeated bills to create one have failed.

== 2.4 Stills and clips: a different question, and a worse answer ==

The two cases everyone cites are both Ninth Circuit and both about '''search engines'''.

'''Kelly v. Arriba Soft Corp., 336 F.3d 811 (9th Cir. 2003)''' (amending 280 F.3d 934 (9th Cir. 2002)).
A photographer sued an image search engine that displayed '''thumbnails''' of his pictures. Held: the
thumbnails were '''prima facie infringing but fair use''' — the use was transformative, serving an
indexing function rather than an aesthetic one, and the low-resolution thumbnails did not substitute
for the originals. Critically, the 2003 amended opinion '''withdrew''' the 2002 holding on the
'''full-size inline-linked/framed images''' and remanded it: the court declined to decide that the
display of full-size images was infringing or fair.

'''Perfect 10, Inc. v. Amazon.com, Inc., 508 F.3d 1146 (9th Cir. 2007)''' (amending 487 F.3d 701).
Held: Google's thumbnails in image search were '''highly transformative''' — a "new and socially
beneficial function" improving access to information — and that transformative character outweighed
the commercial nature of the use; Perfect 10 failed to show significant market harm. Separately held
that '''in-line linking and framing a full-size image hosted elsewhere is neither a "display" nor a
"distribution"''' by the linking site (the "server test").

'''Here is the honest reading, and it is not the one the operator is hoping for.'''

Both cases turn on a '''search engine indexing the open web''': an automated, comprehensive, neutral
pointer whose entire social value is ''sending the user to the original''. Neither case authorises a
'''curated library of screenshots offered as the product itself'''. Walk the four factors for a
subscription site whose screenshots ''are'' what people pay for:

* '''Purpose and character.''' A thumbnail in a search index is transformative because its function
  differs from the original's. A screenshot of a scene, presented to a user who came specifically to
  see that scene, performs '''the same function the film performs'''. That is the opposite of
  transformative, and the commercial character is direct and substantial.
* '''Nature of the work.''' Feature films are core creative expression. Factor against.
* '''Amount and substantiality.''' Small in the quantitative sense — but ''Harper & Row'' makes
  qualitative substantiality decisive, and a curated index selects precisely the scenes with the
  highest draw. Taking the "heart" of the thing you took is the worst version of this factor.
* '''Market effect.''' The commentary-and-criticism argument is genuinely available here and should not
  be dismissed — written criticism of a film, quoting a frame to illustrate a point, is textbook
  fair use. But the argument degrades sharply with volume and with resolution, and it collapses
  entirely when the media is behind a paywall and the text around it is pretextual.

'''Where I think the line falls:'''

{| class="wikitable"
!  !! Assessment
|-
| Metadata index, no media — title / performer / timestamp / your own factual descriptor || '''Defensible.''' Feist. Not a reproduction of anything.
|-
| Linking out to a licensed source (studio page, JustWatch, a streaming deep-link) || '''Defensible.''' No copy is made.
|-
| Official promotional stills and press-kit images used within their press terms || '''Defensible, within the terms.''' Press kits grant editorial use; a paywalled gallery usually exceeds it. Read each one.
|-
| A frame or two illustrating genuine written criticism, free side, low-res || '''Arguable fair use''', strongest where the text is real and substantial. Not a product.
|-
| A curated, paywalled library of screenshots as the primary draw || '''Not defensible.''' No case supports it. Kelly and Perfect 10 do not reach it.
|-
| Hosted video clips || '''Not defensible.''' This is straightforward reproduction and public performance of audiovisual work.
|}

The incumbent has run the bottom two rows for 26 years on an untested theory and an unenforced
tolerance. That is a fact about enforcement appetite, not about the law.

== 2.5 Right of publicity — the exposure the question did not ask about ==

This is '''separate from copyright''', it is '''state law''', it survives the copyright analysis
entirely, and in this specific business it is the one that actually bites.

* There is '''no federal right of publicity'''. Roughly 30 states plus DC recognise one, about 19 by
  statute, the rest at common law; all 50 have ''something'' under the privacy label. Every one of them
  is different.
* '''California Civil Code §3344(a)''': liability for knowingly using another's "name, voice,
  signature, photograph, or likeness" for purposes of advertising or selling without prior consent.
  The Celebrities Rights Act (1985, now §3344.1) gives a '''70-year post-mortem''' right.
* '''New York Civil Rights Law §§50–51''' (consent required for use for advertising or trade), plus
  '''§50-f''' (added 2020, see below) and '''§52-c'''.
* '''Indiana and Oklahoma: 100 years post-mortem.''' Indiana's statute reaches signature, photograph,
  gestures, distinctive appearance and mannerisms. '''Tennessee's right does not expire while use is
  continuous.''' These are the forum-shopping states.
* The only Supreme Court decision is '''Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broadcasting Co., 433 U.S. 562
  (1977)''': the First Amendment did '''not''' shield a broadcaster who aired a performer's entire act
  without consent. That is a narrow holding, but it is the one on point for "we reproduced the
  performance itself."
* '''Defences:''' newsworthiness and matters of public concern; the transformative-use test (*Comedy
  III Productions v. Gary Saderup*, 25 Cal. 4th 387 (2001)); artistic relevance (*ETW Corp. v. Jireh
  Publishing*, 332 F.3d 915 (6th Cir. 2003); ''Brown v. Electronic Arts'', 724 F.3d 1235 (9th Cir.
  2013)). Courts have often treated editorial publication as non-commercial for these purposes.
* '''Copyright preemption (17 U.S.C. §301)''' is the live doctrinal fight and it cuts for you on the
  media and against you on the marketing. ''Laws v. Sony Music Entertainment'', 448 F.3d 1134 (9th Cir.
  2006): a publicity claim that is in substance about the reproduction of a '''copyrighted recording
  of a performance''' is preempted. ''Toney v. L'Oréal USA'', 406 F.3d 905 (7th Cir. 2005): a claim about
  the '''identity/persona''' itself is '''not''' preempted, because identity is not fixed in a tangible
  medium. Translating: a performer complaining that you reproduced ''the film'' is likely preempted;
  a performer complaining that you used ''her name and face to sell subscriptions'' is not.

'''The specific problem.''' A site of this kind necessarily does two things simultaneously: it
publishes factual/editorial information about performers (protected), and it uses those performers'
names and images to market a paid product (the thing §3344 and §§50–51 were written for). The
