performer index page, the search-engine-facing performer name, the thumbnail on the signup funnel —
those are where a publicity claim lands, and preemption does not save them. '''The editorial framing
is not cosmetic. It is the defence, and it has to be real.'''

'''Outside the US''', there is no general UK image right, but the UK gets there via passing off and
UK GDPR; '''France''' protects image under Article 9 of the Civil Code with a strong independent
''droit à l'image''; '''Germany''' protects image under KUG §§22ff and the general personality right
(Art. 1/2 GG, §823(1) BGB); '''GDPR''' treats a photograph of an identifiable person as personal data
in its own right, which supplies an erasure route (Art. 17) that has nothing to do with copyright or
publicity rights and that a European performer will find far easier to use than a lawsuit.

== 2.6 Where the film data could legitimately come from ==

{| class="wikitable"
! Source !! Verdict for a commercial product
|-
| '''TMDb''' || '''No, without a negotiated agreement.'''
|-
| '''IMDb (free)''' || '''No.'''
|-
| '''IMDb (paid)''' || '''Yes — and it is the closest licensed analogue that exists.'''
|-
| '''Wikidata''' || '''Yes, cleanly.'''
|-
| '''Wikipedia prose''' || '''Facts yes, sentences no.'''
|-
| '''OpenSubtitles''' || '''No. Worst input in the design.'''
|-
| '''First-party observation''' || '''Yes. The only way to get the actual signal.'''
|}

'''TMDb''' — https://www.themoviedb.org/api-terms-of-use (last updated 20 Oct 2023). The licence is
'''non-commercial by default''': §2.A states that the grant "does not permit any commercial use of
TMDB, the TMDB APIs, or TMDB Content," and that commercial use "is only permitted under a separate
written agreement," which "may be subject to, among other things, payment of fees." §2.A expressly
names "providing archived or cached data sets containing TMDB Content to another person or entity"
as commercial use. §1.C independently prohibits caching "for longer than 6 months," making
"derivatives of the TMDB APIs or TMDB Content," and use "in connection with, including for training,
a machine learning (ML) or artificial intelligence (AI) based Application." §3 makes attribution
mandatory and two-part: the TMDB logo, "less prominent than" your own marks, plus the notice that
the app "uses TMDB and the TMDB APIs but is not endorsed, certified, or otherwise approved by TMDB."
And §1.C bars use with applications that, "in TMDB's sole discretion," involve "obscene,
pornographic, abusive, or otherwise offensive content" — a unilateral off-switch pointed directly at
this product. On termination (§1.D) you must purge all cached content. The `adult` boolean and
`include_adult` parameter flag ''adult productions'', '''not''' mainstream films containing nude scenes —
it is not the signal this product needs.

'''IMDb''' — https://www.imdb.com/conditions. "You may not use data mining, robots, screen scraping, or
similar data gathering and extraction tools on this site." The site licence is expressly "personal
and non-commercial," and the Services "may not be reproduced, duplicated, copied, sold, resold,
visited, or otherwise exploited for any commercial purpose" without express written consent.
'''Scraping IMDb is out.''' The free datasets at https://datasets.imdbws.com/ (per
https://data.imdb.com/non-commercial-datasets/) are "available to customers for personal and
non-commercial use" — '''confirmed non-commercial, cannot be used here''' — and in any case contain no
scene-level or timecode data. '''The commercial route is real and is the interesting finding:''' IMDb
licenses ''IMDb Essential Metadata'', ''IMDb Ratings'', ''Box Office Mojo'', and add-on datasets including
'''Parents Guide — "severity ratings and scene descriptions of adult/potentially-harmful on-screen
content and themes."''' That is the closest thing to a licensed version of the target signal that
exists anywhere. Distribution is via '''AWS Data Exchange'''; a GraphQL API is available exclusively
through it. '''No public pricing — contact sales.''' (https://data.imdb.com/)

'''Wikidata''' — https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Licensing. Structured data in the main,
Property, Lexeme and EntitySchema namespaces is '''released into the public domain under CC0 1.0'''.
Film and cast statements (P161 cast member, P57 director, etc.) are therefore '''commercially
reusable with no legal attribution obligation'''. CC0 is a waiver, not a conditioned licence: no
share-alike, no notice duty. SPARQL at `https://query.wikidata.org/sparql`; dumps at
`dumps.wikimedia.org`; Action API, Wikibase REST/GraphQL, and EventStreams also available. Observe
the Wikimedia User-Agent policy, honour `429`/`Retry-After`, send `Accept-Encoding: gzip,deflate`.
'''This is the clean spine for the film/cast graph.'''

'''Wikipedia prose''' — https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use §7. Text is
dual-licensed '''CC BY-SA 4.0 and GFDL'''. §7.7 requires attribution by hyperlink/URL to the reused
page, or to a stable free copy, or by listing all authors; §7.8 requires modified/added content to
go out under CC BY-SA 4.0 or later with a licensing notice. '''Copying Wikipedia sentences drags a
viral share-alike obligation into your database. Extract facts, write your own prose.'''

'''OpenSubtitles''' — I could not verify the current terms: opensubtitles.com and .org returned HTTP
403 to every automated fetch. More importantly, '''the copyright question is already decided against
reuse in at least one EU jurisdiction.''' Subtitles are a transcription/translation of the dialogue —
a '''derivative work of the screenplay''' — and in '''Stichting Laat Ondertitels Vrij v. BREIN'''
(Rechtbank Amsterdam, ~20 April 2017) the court rejected every claim by the fansubbing foundation
and held that subtitles may be created and distributed '''only with the rightsholders' permission''',
so unauthorised fan subtitles — including freely given ones — infringe. It is a Dutch first-instance
judgment, binding on the parties, but it is the leading authority in Europe and persuasive. '''Using
community subtitle files for timecode alignment imports a judicially-established infringement risk
into the core of the product.''' Do not.

== 2.7 Synthetic/deepfake law — the thing that changes the tolerance ==

A property in this space will be targeted with synthetic imagery whether or not it wants it, and the
law landed in 2025.

'''ENACTED, federal — TAKE IT DOWN Act, S.146, Pub. L. 119-12, signed 19 May 2025.'''
(https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ12/html/PLAW-119publ12.htm)
* Amends 47 U.S.C. §223 to criminalise knowingly publishing an intimate visual depiction of an
  identifiable adult, without consent and causing harm, via an interactive computer service; a
  parallel offence covers minors. Threats to publish are also covered.
* '''Digital forgeries are covered on the same terms''' — defined as an intimate visual depiction
  created through software or machine learning that a reasonable person would take to be authentic.
* Penalties: up to '''2 years''' (adult victim), up to '''3 years''' (minor victim), plus fines.
* '''§3 platform duty:''' covered platforms must operate a reporting process and remove a reported
  depiction '''"as soon as possible, but not later than 48 hours,"''' plus make reasonable efforts to
  remove known identical copies. Good-faith removals are shielded.
* '''"Covered platform" (§4)''' is the clause to read twice: a public-facing site/service/app that
  either primarily hosts user-generated content '''or regularly publishes or makes available
  non-consensual intimate depictions as part of its business.''' The second limb is not limited to
  UGC sites.
* '''Enforcement is by the FTC''', as an unfair or deceptive act or practice. '''No private right of
  action.'''
* '''Compliance deadline was ~19 May 2026 — already passed.''' Any covered platform is inside the
  enforcement window now, not later.

'''PENDING, federal (not law as of this memo):'''
* '''DEFIANCE Act''' — civil remedy for victims of non-consensual sexually explicit digital forgeries.
  Passed the '''Senate by unanimous consent 13 January 2026'''; House companion '''H.R. 3562''' still in
  House Judiciary as of mid-July 2026. '''Not enacted.'''
* '''NO FAKES Act''' (federal digital-replica right in voice and likeness) — '''S.4591 / H.R.8915''',
  reintroduced 20 May 2026, out of Senate Judiciary unanimously 18 June 2026, '''stalled on the Senate
  floor''' since a 7 October 2026 objection on First Amendment grounds. Includes a DMCA-style
  counter-notification process. '''Not enacted.'''

'''ENACTED, states (the ones that matter here):'''
* '''New York CRL §50-f and §52-c''' (S5959-D, signed 30 Nov 2020, Ch. 304). §50-f: 40-year
  post-mortem right for deceased performers/personalities, expressly covering '''digital replicas'''.
  §52-c: private right of action for a "depicted individual" against unconsented dissemination of
  sexually explicit material, with consent required in a '''signed, plain-language agreement'''
  rescindable within three business days; "digitization" is defined to cover realistically depicting
  another person's nude body parts as the depicted individual's. Remedies include punitive damages
  and fees. Exemptions for legal proceedings, matters of legitimate public concern and newsworthy
  works. Limitation: later of 3 years from dissemination or 1 year from discovery.
* '''New York GOL §5-302''' (S7676-B, signed 13 Dec 2024, eff. 1 Jan 2025) — voids digital-replica
  contract clauses absent a reasonably specific description of use '''and''' counsel or union
  representation.
* '''New York S.8420''' (signed 11 Dec 2025, eff. ~June 2026) — advertisers with actual knowledge that
  an ad features a '''"synthetic performer"''' must conspicuously disclose it; $1,000 first violation,
  $5,000 thereafter. '''S.8882''' extends the deceased-personality right to digital replicas.
* '''California Civil Code §1708.86''' (AB 602, 2019, Ch. 491) — civil action for creating and
  disclosing, or knowingly disclosing, sexually explicit material without consent, expressly
  reaching digitally altered content; carve-outs for legitimate public concern and protected
  commentary; statutory and punitive damages plus fees.
* '''California AB 1831''' (2024, Ch. 926) — extends CSAM prohibitions to AI-generated material.
* '''Tennessee ELVIS Act''' (signed 21 Mar 2024, eff. 1 July 2024) — adds voice to the protected
  attributes, and notably attaches liability to '''distributing a tool whose primary purpose is
  producing a particular identifiable individual's likeness''' where unauthorised use is known. Civil
  remedies plus Class A misdemeanour.

'''Build consequence, not a nicety:''' if the property has '''any''' user-contributed surface — comments
with images, submissions, avatars, a tip line — it should be designed from day one with a TAKE IT
DOWN-compliant intake and '''48-hour removal''' path, identical-copy detection, and a logged
takedown ledger. Retrofitting it after a complaint is how an FTC matter starts.

---

'''PART 3 — THE BOTTOM LINE'''

== 3.1 Launch immediately, zero rights risk, zero cost ==

A fine-art nude gallery sourced from '''CC0 museum open access'''. The three to build on first are the
'''Metropolitan Museum''', the '''Getty''', and the '''Cleveland Museum of Art''' — all three CC0, all
three stating commercial use in their own words, none requiring attribution, all three reachable
without negotiation. Getty's page is the most explicit of any institution surveyed (*"may be used
without restriction or fees for commercial and noncommercial purposes"*), and its 86,000+ Museum
images include the '''19th-century photography''' that is the heart of §1.6. Cleveland's API is the
cleanest machine interface (`share_license_status == "CC0"`). The Met has the largest CC0 set and a
CSV dump.

Add immediately after, all verified and all commercially clear: '''National Gallery of Art''' (CC0,
explicitly "commercial or non-commercial"), '''Smithsonian''' (CC0), '''Rijksmuseum''' (CC0 on PD
reproductions), '''Paris Musées''' (CC0, 420,243 PD images), '''SMK Denmark''' (Public Domain Mark,
153,227 PD records), '''Nationalmuseum Sweden''', and the '''Finnish National Gallery''' (CC0, 36,000+).
Together that is a very large body of painting, drawing, print, sculpture and early photography in
the academic-nude and classical-figure tradition, available this week, with no licence to negotiate
and no fee to pay.

'''Do not include in the first build:''' Art Institute of Chicago (image licence unverified), Yale
(commercial use unstated), Harvard (non-commercial plus a decency clause), British Museum (NC),
Louvre and Gallica (commercial use is paid), and anything sourced from an Italian State institution
(§1.6.5).

Five engineering requirements that are not optional:
# '''Allow-list the rights value at ingest''' (`CC0` / `PDM` / `NoC-US` / `CC BY` / `CC BY-SA` only),
   and reject everything else — every `NC`, every `ND`, every `InC-*`, `CNE`, `UND`, `NoC-NC`,
   `NoC-OKLR`.
# '''Honour the per-object flag, not the institutional policy.''' `isPublicDomain` at the Met,
   `share_license_status` at Cleveland, `is_public_domain` at AIC, `public_domain` at SMK. A general
   CC0 policy does not make every image in a collection CC0.
# '''Store provenance per image''' — source URL, institution, rights value ''as it read on the day'',
   object/accession ID, fetch date. This is the entire defence if a claim is ever made, and it
   cannot be reconstructed later.
# '''Mechanically generate attribution''' for any CC BY / CC BY-SA item, from the database record, so
   that it is impossible to publish one without its credit (CC BY §6(a) terminates automatically on
   any failure to comply).
# '''Watch for the metadata defect.''' Cleveland flags Brigman's 1909–12 ''Camera Work'' gravures and
   an 1895 F. Holland Day print as `Copyrighted` while flagging the same bound volume and the
   Clarence White plates `CC0`. The `Copyrighted` flags are wrong as a matter of law. '''Respect the
   flag anyway at ingest''' — an automated filter should never second-guess a source — but log the
   rejects for human review rather than losing them, and raise the inconsistency with Cleveland.

== 3.2 Needs licensing ==

* '''Contemporary photography.''' There is no free route. Either commission it under a work-for-hire
  agreement with model releases, or licence it. Commissioning is cheaper than it looks and is the
  only path that gives you clean title ''and'' releases ''and'' 2257-compliant paperwork in one
  transaction.
* '''Any NC-licensed collection you actually want''' (the British Museum's is the obvious one) —
  negotiate directly.
* '''Mid-century photography (1931–1977).''' Often free via non-renewal, but each item requires a
  renewal search to prove it. That is a research cost, not a licence cost, and it is real.
* '''Film data at scale''', if the Part 2 idea proceeds: an '''IMDb commercial licence via AWS Data
  Exchange''', where the ''Parents Guide'' add-on is the closest licensed analogue to the target signal.

== 3.3 Not worth attempting ==

* '''Anything NC or ND.''' Not a grey area; the licence does not grant the right.
* '''Scraping IMDb.''' Expressly prohibited, trivially detected, and there is a paid route.
* '''Building on TMDb.''' Non-commercial by default, 6-month cache cap, no-derivatives, no-AI, and a
  sole-discretion content clause aimed at exactly this. Even a negotiated agreement leaves them an
  off-switch.
* '''Subtitle files as a timing signal.''' Judicially established infringement risk (BREIN, 2017) at
  the core of the product.
* '''A hosted library of film screenshots or clips.''' See §3.4.
* '''Copying an existing index's taxonomy, ratings or descriptions.''' Take the facts (Feist permits
  it); do not take the selection, arrangement or expression.

== 3.4 The single biggest legal exposure in the Mr. Skin-style idea ==

'''It is not copyright in the films. It is the performers.'''

The copyright exposure is real but bounded and avoidable: drop the hosted stills and clips, keep the
index, and Feist does most of the work. The exposure that does not go away by deleting media is
'''right of publicity''' — a state-by-state, non-preempted claim (''Toney'') that attaches precisely
where this business makes its money: using identifiable performers' names and faces to sell
subscriptions. There is no federal safe harbour, no DMCA-style notice-and-takedown shield, no
registration to rely on, and the post-mortem terms run 70 years in California, 100 in Indiana and
Oklahoma, and potentially forever in Tennessee. A single plaintiff in a favourable forum, with a
statutory-damages hook and fee-shifting, is a materially worse problem than a studio takedown — and
the legislative direction of travel in 2024–2026 (NY §50-f/§52-c, TN ELVIS, NO FAKES if it clears
the floor) is unanimously toward strengthening exactly that claim.

The incumbent's 26 years of survival is tolerance, not precedent. '''If this is built at all, build
the metadata layer only, write your own editorial prose, link out rather than host, and operate a
no-questions-asked per-performer opt-out from day one.''' The opt-out is not a courtesy; it is the
cheapest available mitigation of the one claim you cannot structurally defend.

== 3.5 Why "fine art, non-explicit" changes the compliance picture — 18 U.S.C. §2257 ==

This is the operator's whole premise and it is worth being exact, because the statute is narrower
than its reputation.

'''§2257 is triggered by "actual sexually explicit conduct," not by nudity.''' §2257(a)(1) applies to
material containing visual depictions "of actual sexually explicit conduct" made after 1 Nov 1990;
§2257(h)(1) defines that as '''"actual but not simulated conduct as defined in clauses (i) through
(v) of section 2256(2)(A)."'''

'''18 U.S.C. §2256(2)(A)''' defines "sexually explicit conduct" as actual or simulated —
> (i) sexual intercourse, including genital-genital, oral-genital, anal-genital, or oral-anal,
>     whether between persons of the same or opposite sex;
> (ii) bestiality;
> (iii) masturbation;
> (iv) sadistic or masochistic abuse; or
> (v) '''lascivious exhibition of the anus, genitals, or pubic area of any person.'''

(https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/2256 · https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/2257)

'''Mere nudity is not on that list.''' Clauses (i)–(iv) are acts; clause '''(v)''' is the only one that
could reach a still image of an unclothed person, and it requires '''"lascivious exhibition"''' — not
exhibition, ''lascivious'' exhibition.

The federal courts assess lasciviousness under the '''''Dost'' factors''' (''United States v. Dost'', 636
F. Supp. 828 (S.D. Cal. 1986)): (1) whether the focal point of the depiction is the genitals or
pubic area; (2) whether the setting is sexually suggestive, i.e. a place or pose generally
associated with sexual activity; (3) unnatural pose or inappropriate attire; (4) full or partial
nudity; (5) whether the depiction suggests sexual coyness or willingness to engage in sexual
activity; (6) whether it is intended or designed to elicit a sexual response in the viewer. Two
caveats on ''Dost'': it arose in a child-exploitation prosecution and is phrased in those terms, so
courts adapt it when applying §2256(2)(A)(v) to adults; and the factors are '''"neither comprehensive
nor necessarily applicable in every situation"''' (''United States v. Amirault''), with no requirement
that all six be met.

'''Nudity is a single factor among six, and factor (4) alone does not get there.''' A classical or
academic nude — the whole figure, a studio or landscape setting, conventional art-historical
framing, no focal emphasis on the genitals, no suggestion of sexual activity or coyness — fails
factors (1), (2), (3), (5) and (6), and is '''not''' a lascivious exhibition under any ordinary
application of the test.

'''So the compliance delta is large:'''

{| class="wikitable"
!  !! Explicit content property !! Fine-art nude property
|-
| §2257 producer records (name, DOB, all aliases, from an ID document, held at business premises, available for inspection) || '''Required''' || '''Not triggered''' by non-lascivious nudity
|-
| §2257(e) label on every copy stating where records are kept || '''Required''' || '''Not triggered'''
|-
| §2257A (simulated conduct) || May apply || Not triggered
|-
| 28 C.F.R. Part 75 regime, primary/secondary producer duties || Applies || Does not apply
|-
| Payment processors / card-scheme adult rules || Adult-flagged, high-risk MIDs, reserves || Ordinary processing, '''if''' positioning holds
|-
| App-store, ad-network and platform policy || Largely closed || Largely open
|}

Two cautions, because the gap between "not triggered" and "safe" is where people get hurt:

# '''The statute's threshold is judged on the material, not on your positioning.''' Calling the
   property fine art does not change the §2256(2)(A)(v) analysis; the images do. '''If the editorial
   line ever drifts — close-cropped genital focus, sexually suggestive staging, "artistic" as a
   label over material that is doing something else — the statute attaches, retroactively, to
   material already published, and the records that would satisfy it do not exist.''' The correct
   control is an '''ingest policy with a written standard and a human reviewer''', not a disclaimer.
# '''For historic public-domain material §2257 is irrelevant in any event''' (the statute reaches
   depictions made after 1 Nov 1990), but '''the commissioned contemporary work in §3.2 is not
   historic.''' Anything you commission should come with model releases, age verification and ID
   records '''regardless''' of whether §2257 is triggered — because it is near-free to do at the point
   of commission, impossible to do afterwards, and it is also the evidence that defeats a
   right-of-publicity or consent claim. Treat it as standard production hygiene, not as a §2257
   admission.

'''Constitutional status of §2257''', since it comes up: the Third Circuit in *Free Speech Coalition v.
Attorney General*, 825 F.3d 149 (3d Cir. 2016) (en banc) upheld the record-keeping requirements
against First Amendment challenge but held that '''warrantless inspection of records at any time
violates the Fourth Amendment.''' The Sixth Circuit upheld the statute en banc in 2009 and certiorari
was denied. '''The record-keeping regime is good law.''' Do not plan around it falling.

These are open items, flagged rather than guessed:

`britishmuseum.org`, `pro.europeana.eu`, `musee-orsay.fr`, `gallica.bnf.fr`,
`digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de`, `imogencunningham.com`, `eur-lex.europa.eu`. Where a working route to
the same institution's own data existed (the AIC, Europeana, SMK and Met APIs; the EU Publications
Office CELLAR endpoint; Getty's project page) it was used and is cited as such.

# '''Art Institute of Chicago — the one real gap in Part 1.''' Metadata terms are verified from the
   live API; the '''image''' licence is not. Someone must open
   https://www.artic.edu/open-access/public-domain and https://www.artic.edu/image-licensing in a
   browser. Do not assume CC0 on images.
# '''National Gallery of Art.''' The CC0 policy and the "commercial or non-commercial" language in
   §1.1 come from search results quoting NGA's own pages, not from the pages themselves — every
   `nga.gov` path returned 403. The GitHub dataset's CC0 licence is directly verified. '''Confirm the
   image policy in a browser''', and note that NGA's rights position on the Stieglitz Key Set
   specifically could not be established at all.
# '''The Met's dedicated image-terms page''' (`metmuseum.org/information/terms-and-conditions/image-resources`)
   returned HTTP 429 on every attempt. The CC0 waiver and commercial permission quoted in §1.1 come
   from the Met's own Open Access dataset repository, which is primary, but read the image page once
   before ingest.
# '''Smithsonian.''' CC0 is verified from the Smithsonian's own (now archived) GitHub repository and
   the AWS Open Data registry; `si.edu/openaccess` itself returned 403. Whether the SAAM Muybridge
   plates specifically carry Open Access CC0 is unconfirmed.
# '''Yale's position on commercial use''' — unstated, needs to be obtained in writing.
# '''Orsay / RMN-GP and the live Gallica conditions page''' — terms unverified; the positions in
   §1.2b are the established understanding, not a reading of the current pages.
# '''Rijksmuseum's licence on RP-F-2001-4-34''' (the Igout album) — the record offers a download but
   states no licence.
# '''Princeton University Art Museum's image-rights policy''' — the object API exposes no rights
   field and no policy page could be found. Unknown; must be asked.
# '''Boston Public Library / Digital Commonwealth's Muybridge rights statement''', and '''Heidelberg's
   licence on the ''Camera Work'' scans''' (the TEI transcription dataset is CC BY-SA 4.0; the scan
   licence is not stated).
# '''Two renewal searches would materially change answers and are worth commissioning:''' Alfred
    Cheney Johnston's 1931–1963 published work, and any '''US''' editions of John Everard's titles — a
    failed renewal would move a title out of the URAA bucket into the public domain. 1931–77
    renewals are in the Catalog of Copyright Entries, scanned at
    https://onlinebooks.library.upenn.edu/cce/.
# '''Factual gaps in §1.6:''' whether Alinari actually holds Gloeden material; whether the Nevada
    Museum of Art holds a Brigman archive (their own page points to the Wilson Centre for
    Photography, London); who administers the Gerhard Riebicke ''Nachlass'' (a credited ''Nachlass''
    implies an active claimant on the 1930s work); '''John Everard's death date''' — the single fact
    the UK term depends on; Kurt Reichert's identity and dates; Wilhelm von Plüschow's life dates
    from a primary source; any institutional holding at all for Albert Arthur Allen.
# '''Questions for counsel:''' the French ''prorogations de guerre'' as applied to the Biederer
    material; the French anonymous/pseudonymous rule applied image by image to the Ostra imprints;
    and whether the Italian ''Codice'' regime survives DSM Article 14.
# '''OpenSubtitles' current terms''' — all four primary URLs returned HTTP 403. Everything said about
   their terms is secondary and partly dated; the ''copyright'' analysis (BREIN 2017) does not depend
   on it.
# '''Creative Photographers, Inc. v. SK Intertainment''' — filing confirmed (C.D. Cal., Jan 2019) from
   trade press only. '''Disposition unknown.''' PACER/CourtListener would settle it.
# '''Any right-of-publicity litigation against Mr. Skin''' — none found. That is absence of evidence
   from a rate-limited search, not a finding of none. A PACER name search is the proper check.
# '''Mr. Skin's current ownership''' beyond SK Intertainment, Inc. — unverified.
# '''California AB 621 (2025-26)''' — would extend Civ. Code §1708.86 to minors at creation and to
   knowing facilitators. '''Enactment status unconfirmed.''' Check leginfo.legislature.ca.gov.
# '''Directive 96/9/EC Articles 3, 7, 10, 11''' — EUR-Lex would not render for automated fetch; the
   Article 7 "substantial investment in either the obtaining, verification or presentation of the
   contents" language is verbatim, the rest is close paraphrase from legislation.gov.uk's rendering
   of the same articles. Confirm against EUR-Lex before relying on the exact wording.
# '''Subject-level volume estimates''' in the §1.1 table. No institution publishes a count of
   nude/figure works; those figures are collection-size orders of magnitude, not audited counts.
# '''Image-level rights for any specific object.''' Every claim in this memo is about an
    institution's ''general policy''. The per-object rights field always governs and must be honoured
    at ingest. A general CC0 policy does not make every image in the collection CC0.
